title: Cleopatra lived closer to the Moon landing than to the pyramids
body: The Great Pyramid of Giza was finished around 2560 BC. Cleopatra died in 30 BC, roughly 2,500 years later, and the Moon landing came about 2,000 years after her.
hook: Ancient Egypt was already ancient to the ancient Egyptians.

title: Oxford University is older than the Aztec Empire
body: Teaching at Oxford was underway by 1096. The Aztec city of Tenochtitlan was founded in 1325, more than two centuries later.
hook: "Old" and "new" world timelines overlap in surprising ways.

title: The shortest war lasted under an hour
body: The Anglo-Zanzibar War of 27 August 1896 ended after roughly 38 to 45 minutes of British naval bombardment. The Sultan's palace was wrecked and a pro-British ruler installed.
hook: Power gaps can make conflicts brutally brief.

title: Napoleon was not unusually short
body: He was about 5 feet 7 inches, average for a Frenchman of his time. The myth grew from confusion between French and English inches and from British cartoons mocking him.
hook: Propaganda can outlive the person it targets.

title: The Great Fire of London had few recorded deaths
body: The 1666 fire destroyed around 13,000 houses and St Paul's Cathedral, yet only a handful of deaths were officially recorded. Historians think the true toll among the poor was higher but went uncounted.
hook: Who gets counted shapes what history remembers.

title: Vikings did not wear horned helmets
body: No horned helmet has been found from a Viking-age warrior grave. The image comes largely from 19th-century art and costume design, including Wagner's opera productions.
hook: Much of our picture of the past is Victorian stagecraft.

title: The printing press spread faster than you would think
body: Gutenberg printed his Bible around 1455. By 1500, presses operated in more than 250 European towns and had produced millions of books.
hook: New information technology has always spread fast.

title: Ancient Romans used a kind of concrete that lasts
body: Roman builders mixed lime with volcanic ash. Some harbour structures have survived 2,000 years of seawater, and researchers think minerals growing inside the concrete help seal cracks.
hook: Old techniques can still teach modern engineers.

title: The Hundred Years' War lasted 116 years
body: The conflict between England and France ran from 1337 to 1453. It was a series of wars broken by truces, not one continuous fight.
hook: Historians name periods after the fact, not neatly.

title: Tsar Peter the Great taxed beards
body: In 1698 Peter imposed a tax on beards to push Russian nobles towards Western European fashion. Payers carried a token proving they had paid.
hook: Rulers have long used taxes to change behaviour.

title: The Black Death killed around a third of Europe
body: Between 1347 and 1351 plague swept Europe, killing an estimated 30 to 50 percent of the population. Labour shortages afterwards pushed up wages for surviving workers.
hook: Catastrophes can shift economic power.

title: The Eiffel Tower was meant to be temporary
body: Built for the 1889 World's Fair, it had a 20-year permit. It was saved partly because it proved useful as a radio transmission tower.
hook: Usefulness is a strong defence against demolition.

title: Ancient Olympians competed naked
body: In the ancient Greek Games, male athletes competed nude. The word "gymnasium" comes from the Greek "gymnos", meaning naked.
hook: Words carry fossils of old customs.

title: The Rosetta Stone unlocked hieroglyphs
body: Found in 1799, the stone carries the same decree in hieroglyphs, Demotic and Ancient Greek. Jean-François Champollion used it to announce his decipherment in 1822.
hook: One translated text can open a whole lost language.

title: Mammoths were still alive when the pyramids were built
body: A small population of woolly mammoths survived on Wrangel Island in the Arctic until about 4,000 years ago. The Great Pyramid was built around 4,500 years ago.
hook: Extinction is often a slow fade, not a single event.

title: The first known strike was in ancient Egypt
body: Around 1157 BC, tomb builders at Deir el-Medina stopped work because their grain rations were late. Records of the protest survive on papyrus.
hook: Workers have bargained over pay for over 3,000 years.

title: The Library of Alexandria declined slowly
body: There was no single fire that destroyed everything. The library faded over centuries through funding cuts, political purges and several conflicts.
hook: Institutions usually die from neglect, not drama.

title: Sliced bread was briefly banned in the US
body: In January 1943 the US banned sliced bread to save resources during the war. Public outcry got the ban lifted within about two months.
hook: Small comforts can carry big political weight.

title: Medieval people did not think the Earth was flat
body: Educated Europeans in the Middle Ages generally knew the Earth was round. The flat-Earth myth about them was popularised in the 1800s.
hook: Each era likes to think the last was more ignorant.

title: The Great Wall is not visible from the Moon
body: It is very long but only a few metres wide. Astronauts have confirmed it cannot be seen with the naked eye from the Moon.
hook: Big claims deserve a quick check.

title: Coffee houses were nicknamed penny universities
body: In 17th-century England, a penny bought entry and coffee, plus hours of debate and news. Lloyd's of London began in Edward Lloyd's coffee house.
hook: Shared spaces can incubate whole industries.

title: Paper money started in China
body: China was using paper money by the Song dynasty in the 11th century. Europe did not adopt banknotes widely until the 1600s.
hook: Many "modern" inventions are centuries old.

title: The Titanic's sister ship had a long career
body: RMS Olympic, Titanic's near-identical sister, served from 1911 to 1935. She was nicknamed "Old Reliable" and even rammed a German U-boat in 1918.
hook: Fame often goes to the disaster, not the success.

title: The Aztec capital was built on a lake
body: Tenochtitlan stood on islands in Lake Texcoco, linked by causeways. Mexico City sits on the drained lakebed and is sinking as a result.
hook: Cities inherit the choices of their founders.

title: The Romans had fast food counters
body: Pompeii had dozens of thermopolia, street counters serving hot food and drink. Many Romans in cramped flats had no kitchen of their own.
hook: Eating out is as old as city living.

title: Honey never goes off
body: Honey is so low in water and so acidic that bacteria cannot grow in it. Archaeologists have found pots of honey in ancient Egyptian tombs that were still edible.
hook: The right chemistry beats any preservative.

title: Your body has more bacterial cells than you might think
body: Current estimates put the bacteria in and on a human body at roughly the same number as human cells, about 38 trillion. Most live in the gut.
hook: You are an ecosystem, not a single organism.

title: Water can boil and freeze at the same time
body: At its triple point, about 0.01°C and very low pressure, water exists as solid, liquid and gas at once. Scientists use it to calibrate thermometers.
hook: Everyday substances behave strangely at the edges.

title: Bananas are slightly radioactive
body: Bananas contain potassium, and a small fraction of natural potassium is radioactive potassium-40. You would need to eat millions at once for it to matter.
hook: Dose, not presence, decides danger.

title: Glass is not a slow-moving liquid
body: Old church windows are often thicker at the bottom, but that comes from how medieval glass was made and fitted. At room temperature glass would take far longer than the age of the universe to flow visibly.
hook: A tidy explanation is not always the true one.

title: Lightning is hotter than the Sun's surface
body: A lightning bolt can heat the air around it to about 30,000°C. The surface of the Sun is roughly 5,500°C.
hook: Brief events can be astonishingly extreme.

title: Humans share about 60 percent of genes with bananas
body: Many basic cell functions use genes common to almost all living things. Roughly 60 percent of human genes have a recognisable counterpart in bananas.
hook: All life runs on a shared toolkit.

title: Sound travels faster in water than in air
body: Sound moves at about 343 metres per second in air and around 1,480 in water. Whales can hear each other across hundreds of kilometres.
hook: The medium shapes the message.

title: Hot water can sometimes freeze faster than cold
body: This is called the Mpemba effect, after a Tanzanian student who noticed it in 1963. Scientists still argue over when and why it happens.
hook: Simple questions can stay open for decades.

title: Your stomach gets a new lining every few days
body: Stomach acid is strong enough to damage tissue, so the cells lining your stomach are replaced every few days. Mucus adds another protective layer.
hook: Constant renewal is a survival strategy.

title: Diamonds and pencil lead are the same element
body: Both are pure carbon. In diamond the atoms form a rigid 3D lattice; in graphite they form flat sheets that slide over each other.
hook: Structure can matter more than ingredients.

title: Octopuses have three hearts
body: Two hearts pump blood through the gills and one pumps it around the body. Their blood is blue because it uses copper-based haemocyanin to carry oxygen.
hook: Evolution finds more than one way to solve a problem.

title: A teaspoon of neutron star would weigh billions of tonnes
body: Neutron stars pack more mass than the Sun into a ball about 20 kilometres across. A teaspoon of that material would weigh around a billion tonnes or more.
hook: Matter can be crushed beyond imagination.

title: Your brain uses about a fifth of your energy
body: The brain is around 2 percent of body weight but uses roughly 20 percent of the energy you burn at rest. Thinking is expensive.
hook: Intelligence comes at a metabolic cost.

title: Penicillin was found by accident
body: In 1928 Alexander Fleming noticed mould killing bacteria on a dish left out over a holiday. Turning it into a usable medicine took more than a decade of work by others.
hook: Discovery needs luck and long follow-through.

title: Some metals melt in your hand
body: Gallium melts at about 29.8°C, below body temperature. A spoon made of it would melt in hot tea.
hook: "Solid" depends on the temperature you live at.

title: Hiccups may be a leftover from our ancestors
body: One theory links hiccups to breathing reflexes in amphibian ancestors that gulped air and water. The jury is still out.
hook: Our bodies carry echoes of deep evolutionary history.

title: The human eye can detect a single photon
body: Experiments suggest people can sometimes sense a single photon in total darkness. Most of the time, though, the brain filters out such weak signals.
hook: Our senses are sharper than our attention.

title: Mercury thermometers were phased out for safety
body: Mercury is toxic, and broken thermometers could release vapour. Many countries have restricted mercury thermometers, replacing them with digital or alcohol ones.
hook: Safety often wins over tradition, slowly.

title: Air is mostly nitrogen, not oxygen
body: The air you breathe is about 78 percent nitrogen and only about 21 percent oxygen. The rest is mostly argon, with a tiny share of carbon dioxide.
hook: The obvious ingredient is often not the main one.

title: Fingerprints form before birth
body: Ridges on your fingertips form by around the 17th week of pregnancy. Even identical twins have different fingerprints.
hook: Small random differences make us unique.

title: Antibiotics do not work on viruses
body: Antibiotics target structures found in bacteria, such as cell walls. Viruses lack these, so colds and flu are not helped by antibiotics.
hook: The right tool depends on the right diagnosis.

title: Rainbows are actually full circles
body: From the ground, the horizon cuts off the lower half of a rainbow. From a plane you can sometimes see the full circle.
hook: Our viewpoint hides much of the picture.

title: Your bones are constantly being rebuilt
body: Cells in your skeleton break down old bone and lay down new bone all the time. Over about a decade, much of your skeleton is replaced.
hook: Even the solid parts of us are always changing.

title: Atoms are mostly empty space
body: If an atom's nucleus were the size of a marble, the atom would be about the size of a football stadium. Almost all the mass sits in that tiny centre.
hook: Solid things are mostly nothing at all.

title: The world's oldest company ran for over 1,400 years
body: Kongō Gumi, a Japanese temple builder, was founded in 578 AD. It traded independently until 2006, when it was absorbed by a larger construction firm.
hook: Longevity comes from doing one thing well for a very long time.

title: Coca-Cola was first sold as a medicine
body: In 1886 pharmacist John Pemberton sold Coca-Cola in Atlanta as a tonic at soda fountains. It became a mass-market drink through marketing, not medicine.
hook: Products often find their real market by accident.

title: Nokia started as a paper mill
body: Nokia was founded in Finland in 1865 as a pulp mill. Over the next century it moved into rubber, cables and finally mobile phones.
hook: Companies can reinvent themselves many times.

title: The first barcode scanned was on chewing gum
body: On 26 June 1974, a pack of Wrigley's gum was the first product scanned by a UPC barcode at a supermarket in Ohio.
hook: Huge systems often start with a humble test.

title: Post-it Notes came from a failed glue
body: A 3M scientist created a weak, reusable adhesive in 1968 that nobody could find a use for. Years later a colleague used it to stop bookmarks falling out of his hymn book.
hook: A failure in one context can be a hit in another.

title: Supermarkets put milk at the back for a reason
body: Essentials like milk are often placed at the far end of the store so shoppers pass more products on the way. Each extra aisle is another chance to buy.
hook: Store layouts are designed, not accidental.

title: The 80/20 rule started with peas
body: Economist Vilfredo Pareto noticed that 20 percent of the pea pods in his garden produced most of the peas. He then found that about 20 percent of people owned 80 percent of land in Italy.
hook: Uneven distributions show up everywhere.

title: Prices ending in 99 really work
body: Studies find that prices like £4.99 often sell better than £5.00 because shoppers anchor on the first digit. This is called the left-digit effect.
hook: Small framing changes move big decisions.

title: Lego nearly went bankrupt in 2003
body: After expanding into too many products, Lego faced heavy losses. It recovered by refocusing on its core bricks and cutting complexity.
hook: Focus can rescue a company that sprawled.

title: Amazon started as an online bookshop
body: When it launched in 1995, Amazon sold only books. Books were easy to ship and had a huge catalogue no physical store could stock.
hook: Start narrow, then expand.

title: Monopoly was originally a warning about landlords
body: The game began as The Landlord's Game, patented by Lizzie Magie in 1904 to show how land ownership concentrated wealth. Later versions dropped the message.
hook: Ideas can be repackaged to mean the opposite.

title: The first credit card was for restaurants
body: Diners Club launched in 1950 as a card for paying at restaurants in New York. It was a charge card, paid off in full each month.
hook: Big financial products often start in one niche.

title: Free shipping thresholds raise basket size
body: Many shoppers add items just to reach a free delivery threshold. Retailers set the line slightly above the typical order.
hook: Thresholds nudge behaviour more than discounts.

title: The decoy effect sells more large drinks
body: When a medium option priced close to the large is added, more people choose the large. The middle option exists mainly to make the big one look good value.
hook: Options can be designed to steer a choice.

title: Netflix once mailed DVDs
body: Netflix began in 1997 as a DVD-by-post rental service. It started streaming in 2007 and kept mailing discs until 2023.
hook: The winning business model may grow inside the old one.

title: The stock market's opening bell is a real bell
body: The New York Stock Exchange rings a bell to open and close trading each weekday. Guests ring it as a publicity event.
hook: Rituals help markets feel orderly.

title: Compound interest is called the eighth wonder
body: Money growing at 7 percent a year doubles roughly every 10 years. Starting earlier matters more than starting bigger.
hook: Time is the most powerful input.

title: Most new restaurants struggle in their first years
body: Studies of restaurant openings find a large share close within the first few years. Thin margins and high fixed costs leave little room for error.
hook: Passion needs a business model behind it.

title: Logos rarely use purple
body: Purple is among the least common main colours in big-brand logos; blue and red dominate. Colour choices signal trust, energy or luxury.
hook: Colour is part of the message.

title: Shipping containers changed world trade
body: Standard steel containers, introduced in 1956, cut the cost and time of loading ships dramatically. Global trade grew as a result.
hook: A boring standard can transform an industry.

title: The paperclip has a surprisingly rich history
body: The familiar double-loop Gem paperclip appeared in Britain in the 1870s and was never patented in its classic form. Many tried to improve it, but the design endured.
hook: Good enough can be unbeatable.

title: Bubble wrap was meant to be wallpaper
body: Inventors in 1957 tried to sell textured plastic as wallpaper. It failed, then found its use protecting fragile goods in shipping.
hook: Keep looking for the job your product does best.

title: Sunk costs trap good decision-makers
body: People keep investing in failing projects because of money already spent. The rational choice looks only at future costs and benefits.
hook: Past spending should not decide future spending.

title: A small loss feels bigger than an equal gain
body: Research by Kahneman and Tversky found losses weigh roughly twice as heavily as gains of the same size. This is called loss aversion.
hook: Framing a choice as a loss changes behaviour.

title: Ford's moving assembly line cut build time sharply
body: In 1913 Ford's moving line cut the time to build a Model T chassis from about 12 hours to around 90 minutes. Prices fell and sales soared.
hook: Process innovation can matter more than product.

title: Trees can share nutrients underground
body: Fungal networks link the roots of many trees in a forest. Through them, trees can exchange water, carbon and nutrients, though how much and why is still debated.
hook: Forests are more connected than they look.

title: Sloths can hold their breath longer than dolphins
body: By slowing their heart rate, sloths can hold their breath for up to about 40 minutes. Dolphins usually surface every 8 to 10 minutes.
hook: Slow living has hidden advantages.

title: Flamingos are pink because of their food
body: Flamingos are born grey. Pigments in the algae and shrimp they eat turn their feathers pink over time.
hook: You really are what you eat.

title: A group of crows is called a murder
body: The term dates back to the 15th century, when groups of animals were given poetic names. A group of owls is a parliament.
hook: Language preserves old superstitions.

title: Cows have best friends
body: Studies found cows show lower stress when paired with a preferred companion. They form close social bonds within herds.
hook: Social needs run deep across species.

title: Bamboo can grow almost a metre a day
body: Some bamboo species can grow up to about 90 centimetres in a single day. It is one of the fastest-growing plants on Earth.
hook: Growth rates can be astonishing when conditions suit.

title: Sea otters hold hands while sleeping
body: Sea otters often float in groups called rafts and sometimes link paws so they do not drift apart. They also wrap themselves in kelp.
hook: Simple habits can solve hard problems.

title: Koalas sleep up to 20 hours a day
body: Eucalyptus leaves are low in nutrients and hard to digest. Koalas save energy by sleeping most of the day.
hook: Diet shapes daily life.

title: Some jellyfish can reverse ageing
body: Turritopsis dohrnii can revert to an earlier life stage when stressed. In theory this cycle could repeat indefinitely.
hook: Nature bends rules we think are fixed.

title: Elephants can recognise themselves in a mirror
body: Asian elephants have passed the mirror test, touching marks on their heads they could only see in a reflection. Few animals pass it.
hook: Self-awareness is not unique to humans.

title: Owls cannot move their eyes
body: Owl eyes are tube-shaped and fixed in their sockets. Instead, owls can turn their heads around 270 degrees.
hook: Limits often drive clever adaptations.

title: Bees communicate with a dance
body: Honeybees perform a waggle dance to tell others the direction and distance of food. The angle of the dance points relative to the Sun.
hook: Information can travel without words.

title: Hummingbirds cannot walk
body: Their feet are tiny and suited for perching, so they shuffle or fly even short distances. Their wings can beat dozens of times a second.
hook: Specialisation has trade-offs.

title: Penguins propose with pebbles
body: Male gentoo penguins search for smooth pebbles to offer females. Pebbles are used to build nests that keep eggs off cold ground.
hook: Courtship often has a practical side.

title: Tardigrades can survive in space
body: These tiny animals, under a millimetre long, survived exposure to the vacuum of space in a 2007 experiment. They can dry out and revive years later.
hook: Toughness comes in very small packages.

title: Crocodiles cannot stick out their tongues
body: A membrane holds a crocodile's tongue to the roof of its mouth. It helps stop water flowing into the throat when it opens its jaws underwater.
hook: Every feature has a reason.

title: The Amazon makes much of its own rain
body: Trees release huge amounts of water vapour through their leaves. This moisture forms clouds and rain over the forest and beyond.
hook: Ecosystems can create their own weather.

title: Seahorse fathers give birth
body: Female seahorses lay eggs in a pouch on the male, who carries them until they hatch. He then releases fully formed young.
hook: Parenting roles vary widely in nature.

title: Garden snails have thousands of teeth
body: A snail's tongue-like radula is covered in rows of tiny teeth, often numbering in the thousands. It scrapes food like a rasp, and worn teeth are replaced.
hook: Small creatures can carry surprising tools.

title: Wombats leave cube-shaped droppings
body: Uneven stiffness in a wombat's intestine shapes its droppings into cubes. They use them to mark territory on rocks and logs.
hook: Even odd details have a mechanism.

title: Giraffes have the same number of neck bones as you
body: Giraffes and humans both have seven neck vertebrae. Each of a giraffe's can be over 25 centimetres long.
hook: Evolution stretches a shared design.

title: Dolphins have names
body: Bottlenose dolphins develop signature whistles that work like names. Others use them to call specific individuals.
hook: Identity matters in social animals.

title: Mushrooms are closer to animals than plants
body: Genetic studies show fungi share a more recent common ancestor with animals than with plants. Like us, they cannot make food from sunlight.
hook: Appearances can mislead classification.

title: Snails can sleep for years
body: In dry conditions, some snails seal themselves in their shells and go dormant. They can stay that way for months, occasionally years.
hook: Waiting can be a survival skill.

title: Butterflies taste with their feet
body: Butterflies have taste receptors on their feet. Landing on a leaf tells a female whether it suits her caterpillars.
hook: Senses can be placed where they are most useful.

title: A day on Venus is longer than its year
body: Venus takes about 243 Earth days to spin once, but only about 225 to orbit the Sun. It also spins backwards compared with most planets.
hook: Our idea of a day is only local.

title: There are more stars than grains of sand on Earth's beaches
body: Astronomers estimate around 10^22 to 10^24 stars in the observable universe. That likely outnumbers all the sand grains on Earth's beaches.
hook: Scale in space defeats intuition.

title: Footprints on the Moon could last millions of years
body: The Moon has no wind or rain to erase them. Unless a meteorite hits, the Apollo astronauts' bootprints will stay for a very long time.
hook: Without weather, history stays put.

title: Space is not completely silent to instruments
body: Sound cannot travel through the near-vacuum of space. But spacecraft record radio waves and plasma vibrations that scientists convert into sound.
hook: Translation reveals hidden signals.

title: Saturn would float in a big enough bath
body: Saturn's average density is lower than water's. In a hypothetical ocean large enough, it would float.
hook: Giant does not always mean heavy for its size.

title: Sunlight takes about eight minutes to reach us
body: Light travels at about 300,000 kilometres per second. From the Sun to Earth, that takes around 8 minutes and 20 seconds.
hook: When you look at the sky, you see the past.

title: The International Space Station orbits every 90 minutes
body: The ISS travels at about 28,000 kilometres per hour. Astronauts on board see around 16 sunrises and sunsets a day.
hook: Speed changes even the rhythm of a day.

title: Mars has the tallest volcano in the solar system
body: Olympus Mons is about 22 kilometres high, more than twice the height of Everest above sea level. Its base is roughly the size of Poland.
hook: Low gravity lets mountains grow huge.

title: Astronauts grow taller in space
body: Without gravity compressing the spine, astronauts can gain up to about 3 percent in height. They shrink back after returning to Earth.
hook: Gravity shapes our bodies every day.

title: A year on Neptune lasts 165 Earth years
body: Neptune is so far from the Sun that it takes about 165 years to complete one orbit. It completed its first orbit since discovery in 2011.
hook: Distance stretches time.

title: Jupiter's Great Red Spot is a giant storm
body: The storm is wider than Earth and has been observed for at least 150 years. It has been shrinking in recent decades.
hook: Some storms outlast centuries.

title: The Moon is slowly drifting away
body: Laser measurements show the Moon moves about 3.8 centimetres further from Earth each year. That is about as fast as fingernails grow.
hook: Tiny changes add up over billions of years.

title: You could fit all the planets between Earth and the Moon
body: The average Earth–Moon distance is about 384,400 kilometres. The diameters of all the other planets add up to slightly less than that.
hook: Space between things is vast.

title: Pluto is smaller than the Moon
body: Pluto's diameter is about 2,377 kilometres, while the Moon's is about 3,475. It was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006.
hook: Categories change as we learn more.

title: Mercury is not the hottest planet
body: Despite being closest to the Sun, Mercury is beaten by Venus. Venus's thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat, keeping it above 460°C.
hook: Insulation matters more than distance.

title: The universe is about 13.8 billion years old
body: Measurements of the cosmic microwave background put the age of the universe at roughly 13.8 billion years. Earth is about 4.5 billion years old.
hook: We are newcomers in a very old story.

title: Voyager 1 is the farthest human-made object
body: Launched in 1977, Voyager 1 entered interstellar space in 2012. It carries a golden record of sounds and images from Earth.
hook: A message in a bottle, sent across the stars.

title: Some planets orbit two suns
body: Astronomers have found planets orbiting pairs of stars. Kepler-16b, found in 2011, was the first clear example.
hook: Science fiction keeps turning into science.

title: Neutron stars can spin hundreds of times a second
body: Pulsars are spinning neutron stars that sweep beams of radiation across space. The fastest known spin over 700 times a second.
hook: Collapse can create extreme spin.

title: There is a giant cloud of alcohol in space
body: Sagittarius B2, a gas cloud near the centre of our galaxy, contains large amounts of ethyl alcohol. It is spread too thin to be drinkable.
hook: Chemistry happens everywhere.

title: The Sun makes up 99.8 percent of the solar system's mass
body: All the planets, moons and asteroids together are a tiny fraction. Jupiter holds most of what is left.
hook: One giant dominates the family.

title: Black holes do not suck everything in
body: From a distance, a black hole's gravity behaves like any object of the same mass. Only very close in, past the event horizon, is escape impossible.
hook: Myths exaggerate the danger.

title: Mars has blue sunsets
body: Fine dust in the Martian atmosphere scatters blue light forward around the Sun. Rovers have photographed bluish sunsets.
hook: Different air paints a different sky.

title: A spoonful of the Sun's core would be scorching
body: The Sun's core is about 15 million degrees Celsius. Nuclear fusion there turns hydrogen into helium.
hook: Stars are nuclear furnaces.

title: Earth is closest to the Sun in January
body: Earth's orbit is slightly oval. It reaches its closest point, perihelion, in early January, during northern winter.
hook: Seasons come from tilt, not distance.

title: "Salary" may come from salt
body: The word comes from the Latin "salarium". A popular story says Roman soldiers were paid in salt, though historians say the link is uncertain.
hook: Good stories cling to words.

title: "Goodbye" means "God be with you"
body: The word is a contraction of the 16th-century phrase "God be with ye". Over time it shortened, influenced by "good day".
hook: Everyday words hide old sentences.

title: "Nice" used to mean foolish
body: In Middle English, "nice" meant silly or ignorant, from the Latin "nescius". Its meaning shifted many times before becoming "pleasant".
hook: Words can flip their meaning entirely.

title: "Quarantine" comes from forty days
body: In 14th-century Venice, ships from plague areas had to wait 40 days before landing. The Italian "quaranta giorni" means forty days.
hook: Public health shaped our vocabulary.

title: English has no official regulator
body: Unlike French, which has the Académie française, English has no official body deciding its rules. Dictionaries record usage rather than dictate it.
hook: English grows by use, not decree.

title: "Robot" comes from a Czech play
body: Karel Čapek's 1920 play R.U.R. introduced the word. It comes from "robota", meaning forced labour.
hook: Fiction often names the future.

title: The dot over an i is called a tittle
body: The small mark over a lowercase i or j is a tittle. It is thought to be where the phrase "to a T" may come from, though that is debated.
hook: Tiny things have names too.

title: "Muscle" means little mouse
body: It comes from the Latin "musculus", little mouse. Romans thought flexing muscles looked like mice moving under the skin.
hook: Body words are full of animal pictures.

title: "Disaster" means bad star
body: It comes from the Italian "disastro", from "dis" (bad) and "astro" (star). Disasters were once blamed on the stars.
hook: Superstition lives on in vocabulary.

title: "Clue" comes from a ball of thread
body: A "clew" was a ball of yarn. In Greek myth, Theseus used thread to find his way out of the labyrinth, so a clew became something that guides you.
hook: Myths become metaphors, then words.

title: Shakespeare is credited with many new words
body: Words like "lonely", "swagger" and "bedroom" first appear in print in his works. Some may simply have been recorded first by him.
hook: First written is not always first said.

title: "OK" started as a joke
body: In 1839, Boston newspapers had a fad for comic abbreviations. "OK" stood for "oll korrect", a deliberate misspelling of "all correct".
hook: Jokes can become global words.

title: Hawaiian has a 13-letter alphabet
body: The Hawaiian alphabet uses five vowels and eight consonants, including the ʻokina glottal stop. Words often repeat sounds.
hook: Small alphabets can carry rich languages.

title: "Sabotage" may come from shoes
body: One theory says it comes from the French "sabot", a wooden clog, linked to workers clumping or disrupting work. The exact origin is debated.
hook: Etymology is often a best guess.

title: "Avocado" comes from an Aztec word
body: The Nahuatl word "āhuacatl" was adapted by Spanish speakers into "aguacate", which became "avocado" in English.
hook: Food words carry trade history.

title: The longest English word in major dictionaries is a lung disease
body: Pneumonoultramicroscopicsilicovolcanoconiosis has 45 letters. It was coined in 1935, partly to be the longest word.
hook: Some words exist just to be records.

title: "Bless you" is said in many languages
body: Many cultures have a response to sneezing, such as "Gesundheit" in German, meaning health. The customs probably grew from wishing good health.
hook: Small rituals unite cultures.

title: "Handicap" came from a betting game
body: "Hand in cap" was a 17th-century trading game. It later described evening out horse races, then disadvantages in general.
hook: Words travel far from their origins.

title: "Ketchup" may come from a fish sauce
body: One theory traces it to a Hokkien Chinese word for a fermented fish sauce. Tomatoes were added much later.
hook: Recipes and words both evolve.

title: Some languages have no words for left and right
body: Guugu Yimithirr in Australia uses compass directions instead, such as north and south. Speakers keep a constant sense of orientation.
hook: Language can shape how we think about space.

title: "Alphabet" comes from its first two letters
body: It comes from Greek "alpha" and "beta", the first two letters of the Greek alphabet. The Greeks adapted them from Phoenician letters.
hook: Names often describe their beginnings.

title: "Hazard" came from a dice game
body: "Hazard" was a medieval dice game, likely from an Arabic word for dice. The meaning shifted from chance to danger.
hook: Risk and games share roots.

title: The ampersand was once a letter
body: "&" comes from a ligature of "et", Latin for "and". Children once recited it at the end of the alphabet as "and per se and".
hook: Symbols can be worn-down words.

title: "Deadline" was once a real line
body: In the American Civil War, a deadline was a boundary in some prison camps that prisoners could not cross. Later it moved into printing and journalism.
hook: Some everyday words have dark origins.

title: Mandarin uses tones to change meaning
body: In Mandarin, the syllable "ma" can mean mother, hemp, horse or scold, depending on its tone. There are four main tones plus a neutral one.
hook: Pitch can carry meaning.
